title: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: floras gain by naturalisation, proportionally with the number of the native genera and species, far more in new genera than in new species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation”. Scope: naturalised plants in regional floras

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-22: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The ratio comparison is explicit and current global flora and alien-species resources contain the needed variables. Taxonomic harmonization is routine and would directly decide the descriptive claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For regional floras, count native and naturalized species and genera and compare proportional additions at each rank, accounting for sampling and taxonomy. A consistently larger proportional gain in genera than species supports the claim; equal or smaller gain refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical introduction effort differs among regions.

Native versus naturalized status and genus boundaries vary among sources.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.78
analysis feasibility: 0.82
data existence: 0.87
discriminating power: 0.84

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparison is a pair of ratios with a pre-registered null, and the regional inventories needed to compute it are public and global. Taxonomic rank is a real artefact, but it is handled inside the same analysis by random draws from the donor pool rather than left as an uncontrolled bias. A small team could confirm or refute the floral generalization with standard checklist joins.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each regional flora, compute the naturalized-to-native ratio at genus rank and at species rank, and compare those ratios with a null that draws the same number of introductions from the global donor pool. A greater proportional gain of genera than of species, beyond that null, would confirm the claim; disappearance of the excess under the null, or across most regions, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Some regions have uneven native inventories.

The pattern for plants need not extend to naturalized animals, which are outside the stated scope.

Genus size and splitting conventions can create an excess of new genera under random introduction.

fields.value:

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For a regional flora, the number of genera added by naturalised (introduced) plants, as a proportion of the native genera, exceeds the number of naturalised species as a proportion of native species.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: WCVP v16 (zip of 2026-06-04) was downloaded; 358,113 accepted non-hybrid species were joined to the level-3 distribution table (location_doubtful rows excluded; a species both native and introduced to an area counted as native). For each of the 337 botanical countries with >= 100 native and >= 20 introduced species, r_sp = introduced/native species and r_gen = genera represented only by introduced species / genera with native species were computed, with the fraction of areas where r_gen > r_sp and the median r_gen/r_sp as the pre-registered statistics. A null expectation for new genera was obtained by 200 random draws per area of the same number of species from all species not native to that area.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. For every TDWG level-3 botanical country in the World Checklist of Vascular Plants with at least 100 native accepted species and at least 20 introduced accepted species, compute r_sp = (introduced species not native to the area) / (native species) and r_gen = (genera represented only by introduced species) / (genera with at least one native species). The claim is SUPPORTED if r_gen > r_sp in at least 80% of qualifying areas AND the median of r_gen / r_sp across areas is at least 1.25.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if r_gen > r_sp in 50% or fewer of qualifying areas, or if the median r_gen / r_sp is 1.0 or less. Intermediate outcomes are 'mixed'. As a secondary, non-decisive analysis, the observed number of new genera per area is compared with the expectation when the same number of species is drawn at random from the global pool of species not native to that area (200 draws per area), to show whether the excess is more than a taxonomic-rank artefact.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of qualifying level-3 areas with r_gen > r_sp

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'naturalisation' is read as the WCVP 'introduced' distribution status (established alien occurrence), his 'flora' as a TDWG level-3 area (the unit of the WCVP distribution table), and 'proportionally with the number of the native genera and species' as the two ratios above. Only accepted species (taxon_rank Species, taxon_status Accepted, no hybrids) are counted; records flagged location_doubtful are excluded. Darwin's own examples are the floras of the United States (Asa Gray's Manual) and Britain; the modern test covers all botanical countries that meet the sample-size rule. Modern reinterpretation: WCVP genus concepts are those of current taxonomy, not of 1859.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Both pre-registered thresholds are met only marginally (0.822 vs 0.80; median ratio 1.2535 vs 1.25), so the descriptive generalisation holds for most floras but the excess of genera is modest, not 'far more' as Darwin wrote; the 95% CI of the fraction of areas is [0.778, 0.859].

The secondary null model points the other way from Darwin's interpretation: in every area, drawing the same number of species at random from the non-native global pool would add more new genera than the real naturalised flora does (observed/expected new genera median 0.61). Naturalised plants are thus more concentrated in genera already native to the recipient flora than random species would be; the r_gen > r_sp pattern is largely an arithmetic consequence of genera being fewer than species, not evidence that naturalised plants are generically distinct from natives.

WCVP 'introduced' covers established aliens as recorded by Kew's editors and is incomplete for some regions (e.g. parts of tropical Asia and the Pacific, where the fraction of supporting areas is lowest); areas are TDWG level-3 units of very unequal size.

Darwin's examples (Gray's 1856 US flora, Britain) used 1850s genus concepts; current genera are narrower and more numerous.
